title: The journey of food
examples: What happens to the food after it leaves the stomach?
How do we get energy from the food we eat?
Which part of the body takes the nutrients from the food?

explain.say: The journey starts in your mouth. Your teeth chew the food up into smaller pieces.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: the digestive system. Look at the oesophagus, the liver and the gall bladder. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
Next, the food travels down the oesophagus. This tube moves the food to the stomach.
In the stomach, strong acids and juices mix with the food. This starts to break down proteins.
Then, the food moves to the intestines. Here, special helpers called enzymes do the real breakdown.
The final important step is absorption. Nutrients pass from the food into your blood to give energy.
When you eat a sandwich, chewing in your mouth starts the long journey. Enzymes help break down the bread and fillings.

faq.q: Where exactly are the nutrients absorbed into the body?
faq.a: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. This is where the digested food passes into your bloodstream.
asks: Which part takes the energy from food?
How do nutrients get into my blood?

faq.q: What is the job of the enzymes in digestion?
faq.a: Enzymes are special juices that help break down large food molecules into tiny pieces. This makes the food usable for your body.
asks: What do enzymes do to food?
Are enzymes like scissors for food?

faq.q: Does the stomach break down everything in the food?
faq.a: No, the stomach mainly breaks down proteins using strong acids. Other parts, like the intestines, handle different types of nutrients.
asks: Is the stomach the only place that digests?
What does the stomach juice do?

faq.q: What happens to the food after it leaves the stomach?
faq.a: It moves into the small and large intestines. Here, more digestion and nutrient absorption continue to happen.
asks: Where does the food go after the stomach?

faq.q: Why do we need the oesophagus?
faq.a: The oesophagus is a muscular tube that pushes the food down from your throat to your stomach. It acts like a slide.
asks: How does food get to the stomach?

facts: Chewing in the mouth breaks food into smaller pieces.
The oesophagus moves food to the stomach using muscle contractions.
The stomach uses acids and enzymes to begin breaking down food.
Nutrients are absorbed through the walls of the intestines into the blood.

quiz.say: Which organ is mainly responsible for absorbing nutrients into the blood?
quiz.why: The small intestine has specialized walls perfect for absorbing nutrients into the bloodstream.

wrong.0: The oesophagus only moves food; it does no digestion or absorption.
wrong.2: Chewing starts digestion, but absorption does not happen here.
wrong.3: The stomach mixes food with acid, but absorption is not its main job.

quiz.say: What is the main function of enzymes in digestion?
quiz.why: Enzymes act like biological scissors, cutting large food items into small, usable parts.

wrong.0: While acids can kill some germs, the main job of enzymes is chemical breakdown.
wrong.1: Taste is determined by chemicals, not the digestive enzymes themselves.
wrong.2: Movement is done by muscles, not the chemical action of enzymes.

quiz.say: If you eat a protein-rich meal, which body part uses acids to start breaking it down?
quiz.why: The stomach is known for its strong acids that begin breaking down proteins.

wrong.0: The small intestine finishes the job, but the stomach starts the protein breakdown.
wrong.1: Saliva in the mouth only starts breaking down starches, not proteins.
wrong.2: The oesophagus is just a passageway and has no digestive juices.
